9.6a — Bias, Filtering & Fair Data

Yesterday's dataset looked scientific. Today the harder question: WHO is in it? Data can be perfectly collected and perfectly wrong, because the sample — not the numbers — carries the bias. This is the IOC-1 core idea on the exam, and it starts with your own playtest pool.

Concept Lab ~15 min

Sampling bias, in your room. Who playtested your cave? Your friends, your table, people who already play platformers. If the class's data says "section 3 is easy," but every tester has 200 hours of Hollow Knight — is section 3 easy? The data is TRUE about the SAMPLE and misleading about the PLAYERS WHO WILL ACTUALLY PLAY. That gap is sampling bias.

BiasIn your project
Selection biasPlaytesters who volunteered are more forgiving (self-selection)
Survivorship biasThe dataset only has rows for testers who FINISHED — quitters left no data
Observer effectTesters play differently when the designer watches (2.4a — why we sit silently)
Confirmation biasYou tune what you already suspected was broken

Filtering — the exam's favorite trap. A filter is a question you ask data: "show me only section 5." Filtering helps see patterns; it can also silently erase people. The classic: "let's drop the outlier runs" — until you realize the dropped runs are all the players who quit, and your average difficulty just got friendlier for no reason.

Socratic

Your class has 30 students; 6 playtested the cave. The dataset says 4.1/5 fun. The exam asks: "Which claim is BEST supported?" — write the cautious version AND the overreaching version of the claim, and say why the exam always wants the first.

Build Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — audit the playtest pool. For the playtests.csv dataset (or your own 7.7a table): list who was IN the sample and what kind of player was NOT. Write one sentence of scope: "This data represents ___, and does not represent ___."

Step 2 — find the missing rows. The dataset has completed_boss = 0 rows. Who is ABSENT entirely? Players who stopped playing mid-cave — no row at all. For each of these absences, name the conclusion that the data would silently get wrong (average rating too high; section times too fast; difficulty curve too flat).

Step 3 — a fair-data fix, in pseudocode. Design the fix the way the exam wants — a filtered average that also REPORTS what it excluded:

kept ← [row FOR row IN runs IF row.completed_boss = 1]
dropped ← [row FOR row IN runs IF row.completed_boss = 0]
DISPLAY("avg win time: " + AVERAGE([row.time_seconds FOR row IN kept]))
DISPLAY("excluded: " + LENGTH(dropped) + " runs")

The second DISPLAY is the ethics: an aggregate that hides its filter is a claim wearing a lab coat.

Step 4 — algorithmic bias preview. Games do this too: your difficulty ramp assumes a player who finished the tutorial. Matchmaking assumes history predicts behavior. Recommendation algorithms trained on biased clicks show more of what was already popular. Same principle, bigger consequences — 9.10a takes it to the real world.

Bug Hunt: Bias in the wild

  1. "95% of surveyed gamers love our game" — the survey was a popup AFTER finishing level 1. Which two biases does that sentence stack?
  2. You drop the slowest 3 runs as "outliers." The average time drops 20%. What did you just prove about section 5 — and about yourself?
  3. The exam classic: a fitness-app dataset comes from phones that track steps. Which population is under-represented, and what will the "average health" numbers claim wrongly?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Scope honestly

  1. Rewrite yesterday's one-sentence insight (9.5a) with its scope clause attached: "…among playtesters who finished the section." What changed in how it sounds?
  2. Design a fairer playtest protocol for the game jam (10.1a): who do you recruit, what do you record, and what do you do about the quitters? Write it in the repo.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Name four biases and find each in a real project's data practice
  • Explain how filtering can silently change a conclusion
  • Write a scoped claim: what the data does and does not represent
  • Pseudocode an aggregate that reports its own exclusions
